entries.title: Art Spiegelman: ‘The US needs a counter-revolution’
entries.summary: More than four decades after his Holocaust story Maus transformed the graphic novel genre, Art Spiegelman discusses Trump, the shadow of 9/11 and the rise of fascism in AmericaWhen the cartoonist Art Spiegelman began dating his future wife, Françoise Mouly, in the mid 70s, she would tell him not to worry about walking her home, because even the New York muggers didn’t bother venturing to where she
entries.content:
When the cartoonist Art Spiegelman began dating his future wife, Françoise Mouly, in the mid 70s, she would tell him not to worry about walking her home, because even the New York muggers didn’t bother venturing to where she lived in Soho. He moved in with her quite suddenly not long after, when his apartment in Greenwich Village burned down. His landlord, who lived on the ground floor, was a hoarder – once, when he came to collect Spiegelman’s rent, a cockroach crawled up from under his shirt collar – and eventually his accumulated junk caught alight.

This feels like a quintessential New York story, but then much of Spiegelman’s life does, or at least fits with the kind of stories we like to tell ourselves about the city. The Soho apartment Spiegelman and Mouly have lived in for five decades is worth millions now and is surrounded by high-end designers; his studio, down the road, is above a branch of Tiffany’s. “It’s just kind of an embarrassment, I mean Tiffany’s is not my class,” says Spiegelman, who refers to these flash new arrivals, dismissively, as “very fancy airport mall stores”.

The couple used to print their own “oddball” comics from a printing press that Mouly, who had dropped out of architecture school in France, installed in their house. Today, they are a New York art establishment power couple. Mouly is the art editor of the New Yorker, having been recruited by Tina Brown in the 90s, when she was looking to make the highbrow magazine “hot”. Spiegelman, who in 1992 became the first cartoonist to win a Pulitzer prize for Maus, a graphic novel about his father’s memories of the Holocaust, has done more than anyone to establish comics as a serious art form, capable of tackling difficult political and personal subjects. The couple’s trajectory had “its own weird logic, although it wouldn’t be anyone else’s. It’s not a ‘recipe for success’,” Spiegelman jokes. “We were wilfully just doing what we wanted to do.”

He is 78 years old, slight and scruffy-looking, with a grizzled goatee and wispy grey hair, and he can still talk faster than most people can think. He offers me a coffee when I arrive at his home on a sweltering June day, but then keeps getting distracted from making it by his own anecdotes. He takes me on an impromptu tour, showing me the living room that held Mouly’s huge, 1,000lb Multilith printing press, until they had a toddler and it became too dangerous to keep. There is a mural painted by the cartoonist Gary Panter on the living room wall, and another just above their bed, painted to replace a set of bookshelves that collapsed on to the couple when they were asleep, breaking Mouly’s nose and prompting a big book clear out. “Is this book worth dying for?” Spiegelman says they asked of themselves, a more hardcore alternative to Swedish death cleaning, but even so there are full bookshelves in every room, and pieces of art and curios everywhere.

As a young man, Spiegelman earned a living designing collectible parody cards for Topps bubblegum, while cutting his teeth in San Francisco’s underground comics scene. After moving to New York, he started Raw magazine with Mouly. Raw published experimental work by comic artists from all over the world, and “it created its own Potemkin village of, yes, all these artists have one thing in common, which is they ain’t like each other,” he recalls. Maus was initially serialised as an insert in Raw – new issues came out sporadically, whenever Spiegelman had finished a chapter.

He struggled to find a publisher for the book, because no one knew what to do with such an unusual work, an autobiographical history of the Holocaust that depicted Jews as mice and Nazis as cats. The responses were “pretty universal that whatever this is, is interesting. But it’s not publishable,” he says. Eventually, Pantheon published it, and Maus became a bestseller. Spiegelman has said he struggled to emerge from the shadow of his best-known creation, but when I ask if he still feels ambivalent about Maus’s success he replies, “I’m ambivalent about absolutely everything … I knew that I wanted it to be read, but it just didn’t occur to me that it would become a phenomenon, it was such an outlier.”

Maus took 13 years to make. For Spiegelman, making comics is often a tortuous process. If many artists complain of creative blocks, then what he experiences is more like a “blockade: there’s no way in or out. I think it’s like a version of impostor syndrome,” he says. “I know I’ve done comics before and they work, but I have no idea how to do it when I start a new one … I have to rethink what it might be to make a comic.” He feels acutely aware of his limitations – “I always understood that I wasn’t the best drawer on the block” – and every square must be painstakingly reworked, dozens of times. “It seems like I don’t function well. I mean, I don’t go: ‘OK, I finished this graphic novel, I’ll do another one – by God!’ – and then off to the races. Something has to make me go through what is such a difficult process for me,” he says.

Spiegelman had virtually stopped making comics and was focused on writing essays and designing covers for the New Yorker when the 9/11 attacks took place. The ground shook, and from his Soho apartment he could see the north tower burning. His first thought was to run to collect his daughter Nadja, who had just started high school at the foot of the towers. Then, fearing that the United Nations might be targeted next, they rushed uptown to collect his son Dash, who was at the UN School. This was the kind of catastrophe his parents, both Auschwitz survivors, had always warned him about, when world history and personal history collide. “I’m not going to get past this unless I start drawing about it,” he realised afterwards, and he vowed to make comics again.

He produced a series about 9/11 for the German magazine Die Zeit, which was later run by other European magazines and American Jewish weekly the Forward. On one page he describes himself as “equally terrorised by al-Qaida and by my own government”. He felt that other American publications were too quiescent in the aftermath of the attacks, and not yet receptive to his fear that the US government was using 9/11 as cover for a massive crackdown on civil liberties and to launch xenophobic wars. “Sigh! It’s hard to be an artist who is consistently Seconds Ahead of His Time,” he writes in the foreword to In the Shadow of No Towers, a book that compiled these comics and is being reissued to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11. (Although, he says, it may come out late – a shipment has been held up in the strait of Hormuz.)

Why was he so alert to the implications for US civil liberties? “Well, my tendency is not to trust the government, so that came easily,” he says. “But it also seems so obvious, like all of a sudden there were police cars and military trucks on Canal Street. We were being told where we could walk, where we couldn’t walk, what we could say, what we couldn’t say. It’s visceral. It’s not like: ‘OK, I’ve read this book on propaganda and here’s how it works.’” Spiegelman notes the direct link between the post-9/11 security crackdowns and some of the excesses of the Trump administration: Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Ice, was created in the aftermath of the terror attacks.

A theme running through Spiegelman’s work is trauma, and its long and toxic aftermath. His parents were Polish Jews who survived the camps but lost most of their family, including their first-born son, Richieu, during the Holocaust. They resettled in Rego Park, Queens, where Spiegelman was born in 1948. In 1968, his mother, Anja, killed herself. Spiegelman was living with his parents at the time, having been hospitalised after suffering a psychotic episode while studying at Harpur College, New York, where he had been experimenting with every drug he could find. Maus is partly about Spiegelman’s fraught relationship with his father Vladek, who is depicted as mean, difficult and racist – a man who complicates the comforting lie we tell ourselves that suffering must make a person kinder or nobler. In one comic, published in Breakdowns (2008), Spiegelman hands a treasure chest to his young son, a family heirloom that was given to him by his own father. Excited, Dash opens the box, only to reveal a terrifying monster. “It’s magical! It makes you feel so worthless you don’t believe you even have the right to breathe,” Spiegelman tells his son, a cigarette hanging from his mouth.

When it comes to 9/11, however, Spiegelman’s perspective has shifted. He no longer views the day as an “end of the world moment”. “It was a big deal. But it was a small big deal compared to the big deals that are going on now,” he tells me. “I’d much rather be in New York than in Iran, for example.”

Around 50 minutes after Spiegelman fires up his Nespresso machine, he finishes making two coffees, and we carry them up to his sunny roof terrace, which as he promised has beautiful views of downtown Manhattan. Spiegelman muses that the US’s volatile politics might reflect humankind’s natural tendency to self-destruction. “I guess, after a while, you get restless, so if you get too comfortable you create problems for yourself, even in more mundane, small-time life, never mind as a nation. At this point, we just had the bad luck of having a megalomaniac walking on to the scene,” he says, of the Trump presidency. American politics is, after all, “entertaining if you don’t give a shit, if you’re nihilistic”.

Spiegelman’s mood is sombre as he discusses how Trump has “very effectively dismantled” the country’s democratic ideals: “Whatever the ideals were, we never lived up to them, but at least we had them. Now it’s all so cynical and sordid and stupid.” The president “is cutting off civil liberties and using his powers to squelch dissent and enrich himself in such thoroughly illegal ways, it’s kind of mindblowing”, Spiegelman says, and he finds himself watching in alarm as the “plutocrat in chief” and his “few dozen toadies” get ever richer while ordinary Americans struggle and suffer a “new indignity every day”. He has no hesitation in describing the Trump administration as fascist. “It’s fascism,” he says. “It’s not nazism, per se, but it has a template that it’s following. And it does have to do with othering, which is the basis of what Maus is about, it’s: ‘OK, you guys are mice, we’re cats.’” Maus is among the many books to be banned by various Republican school boards in recent years, but Spiegelman says he has a “predilection” for producing the kind of art people will seek to ban. Sales of Maus spiked in response to the bans.

“I tend to be pessimistic, but this is worse than most things I know,” he says of American politics. “I just don’t see how we get out of this.” The media are struggling with how to convey the stakes in this post-truth era, he explains, the courts are packed with Trump appointees, democratic norms have been destroyed, and there is no effective opposition. The Republicans are “at this point the equivalent of made men in the mafia,” Spiegelman says, “they’ve committed a murder, they’re complicit in something and they have to keep moving as a complicit unit, so it’s very hard to get someone to blow the whistle and say ‘This is crazy.’” The US needs a “counter-revolution”, Spiegelman says. “But I don’t know where to look for it because the Democrats are so timid.”

An alert sounds on Spiegelman’s phone, and for a moment he is flustered, trying to figure out why on Earth this thing is producing noise. “In some ways I’m slowing down, in other ways I’m still doing what interests me, and sometimes I’m capable of being interested in something more challenging, sometimes less,” he says. He plans, after this interview, to work on a lithograph, his friend having dropped off some stone for him to carve. He hopes to keep living and working in Soho for the rest of his life – but his apartment is a walk-up, and he concedes fate might have other ideas for him. “Anyone can be a genius at 25; at 50 it takes some doing,” Spiegelman writes in one comic. What about at 78, I ask? “I feel like an idiot at this point!” he jokes. “I can’t think the way I thought when I was 25,” he says. He has become more forgetful, for instance, but takes consolation in knowing he can still produce challenging, original art. “There’s still enough wiring that makes it somewhat unorthodox, but I don’t think I’m as far off the grid as I had been.”

entries.title: Rebecca Perry: ‘Lorca hit me like a bolt of lightning’
entries.summary: The poet and novelist on the power of fairytales, being inspired by Frank O’Hara and the joys of Doris LessingMy earliest reading memory Reading On the Ning Nang Nong by Spike Milligan, aged five or so, sitting on the floor of the bedroom I shared with my brother – who, in my memory, was sitting on the carpet next to me.My favourite book growing up I had a collection of fairytales in a big yellow
entries.content:
My earliest reading memory

Reading On the Ning Nang Nong by Spike Milligan, aged five or so, sitting on the floor of the bedroom I shared with my brother – who, in my memory, was sitting on the carpet next to me.

My favourite book growing up

I had a collection of fairytales in a big yellow hardback, which I was totally entranced by from around the age of seven to 10. I’ll never forget the feeling of despair on turning the page and discovering that the Little Mermaid had become foam on the surface of the water; it was a very early lesson in the helplessness of the reader in the face of a story’s destiny. In particular, though, I loved a Scottish fairytale called The Black Bull of Norroway, which I think, in many ways, has been under the surface of everything I’ve ever written.

The book that changed me as a teenager

Collected Plays by Federico García Lorca, which I studied for GCSE drama and led me to seek out his poetry. It would be impossible for me to think about my adolescent relationship to reading, and my relationship as an adult to language, without Lorca. I remember these lines from City That Does Not Sleep hitting me like a bolt of lightning: “… and the man who rushes out with his / spirit broken will meet on the street corner / the unbelievable alligator quiet beneath / the tender protest of the stars”.

The writer who changed my mind

Frank O’Hara, which I know is one of the most predictable answers a poet can give, but for good reason. All of the poetry I’d studied up to the point of discovering him felt deeply serious, almost something not to be touched. Then you read O’Hara and it’s like: OK, life!

The book that made me want to be a writer

I really don’t think this is something that happened to me. I have just written for as long as I can remember and, at a certain point as an adult, I realised that normal living people can write books if they want to, if they’re lucky, and that maybe I would like to try to do that. To answer a slightly different question, Percival Everett’s astonishing The Trees was the book that made me feel I might be able to write a novel.

The book I reread

Anne Carson’s Glass and God, in particular The Glass Essay. It’s basically perfect – my go-to text for resetting my brain and being reminded, within the space of a page, about the capacities of writing.

The book I could never read again

JK Rowling’s Harry Potter series was a huge part of my childhood, but it’s art that’s firmly not to be separated from artist, in this case.

The book I discovered later in life

I don’t think I read Doris Lessing’s The Golden Notebook until I was in my 30s – but really, any time is the perfect time to discover this novel.

The book I am currently reading

A proof of Compensation by Augustine Cerf, which so far is brilliant, and My Garden (Book) by Jamaica Kincaid, which I often pick up and read a page or two of between other things. I’m also rereading Doom Painting by AK Blakemore, out in September. It’s a phenomenal achievement – I don’t know how she did it.

My comfort read

The poetry collection Adam by Gboyega Odubanjo, who died in 2023. I keep this book on the shelf directly above my desk and when the loss of him feels particularly impossible, I take it down, read a poem and remember he’s there on the page.

May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry is published by Granta. It won the 2026 Waterstones debut fiction prize and is longlisted for the Booker prize. To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop.com

entries.title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup
entries.summary: The Amateur by Chris Bohjalian; Claws Out! by Bella Mackie; Plant Lady by Minyoung Kang; Children of Wolves by Lawrence Osborne; Mad Mabel by Sally HepworthThe Amateur by Chris Bohjalian (Hutchinson Heinemann, £18.99) American bestseller Bohjalian deserves to be far better known in the UK, although, as the first line of his 26th novel points out, “It is neither virtue nor might that rules the worl
entries.content:
The Amateur by Chris Bohjalian (Hutchinson Heinemann, £18.99)

American bestseller Bohjalian deserves to be far better known in the UK, although, as the first line of his 26th novel points out, “It is neither virtue nor might that rules the world; it’s luck”. Mira Winston’s luck began early, as she was born into a rich family, clever enough to secure a place at Yale, and a talented enough golfer to consider turning pro, but things change dramatically in 1978 when, at the age of 18, a ball she hits on a driving range smashes the temporal bone of a young caddy, killing him almost instantly. The freak accident turns out to be rather more complicated than first thought, not least because it becomes karmically conflated, in Mira’s mind, with her relationship with a married man twice her age. Told as a memoir, with Mira looking back on the derailment of her life and chronicling society’s changing perceptions of agency and privilege, this literary thriller is a masterfully executed ace.

Claws Out! by Bella Mackie (Borough, £20)

Mackie’s third novel centres on Diana, a manipulative grifter whose previous three husbands have died, apparently of natural causes. She’s in the process of getting her feet under the fourth mark’s prosperous Hampstead table when she encounters opposition. David Farrand’s “entitled but otherwise entirely average” daughter Catriona isn’t going to give up her father or her inheritance without a fight, and when she starts investigating Diana’s past, she discovers that her former stepchildren are convinced of foul play. Meanwhile, Diana’s own son, a feckless charmer, is also hoping to benefit from his mother’s matrimonial plans. Some readers may find the arch authorial tone grating, and the sharp-eyed will spot at least one major plot development before it occurs, but the incisive social satire, vinegary humour and expert pacing will keep you laughing as you turn the pages.

Plant Lady by Minyoung Kang, translated by Shanna Tan (Doubleday, £14.99)

In a fictional Korean city, green-fingered trauma survivor Yoohee realises her dream of opening a plant shop. Although she remains courteous and self-effacing, her long-held conviction that humans, like plants, repay attention and tenderness, has worn thin, and when an errant boyfriend fails to improve, she repurposes him as fertiliser. She begins offering her overwhelmingly female customer base an additional service, ridding them of abusive men, but a young detective notices that the shop is the only common point of reference in a string of otherwise unconnected disappearances, and a game of cat and mouse ensues. This “weird girl” tale of female revenge is politely told, the mechanics of dismemberment happening off the page, and although the villains tend towards the cartoonish, the atmosphere is such that one can almost inhale the damp, scented air of our heroine’s lush botanical haven as she calmly puts the world to rights.

Children of Wolves by Lawrence Osborne (Chatto & Windus, £18.99)

Osborne’s books often feature morally ambiguous expats in exotic locations; here it’s American investigator Tyler Sedgewick, in Turkey to track down Chana Knight at the behest of her father. Posing as a writer, Tyler worms his way into the young woman’s friendship group; Chana, Adam, Diana and Marco are the delinquent, sensation-seeking offspring of wealthy parents, who first met at a California reform school for rich kids, and became self-styled radicals. Now, they have walked out of their respective lives with the intention of atoning for their privileged existences through a “meaningfully violent act” against “a prominent American target”. Tyler, who has become dangerously drawn to Chana, does not realise the extent to which he is being used, and soon attracts the attention of the Turkish intelligence agency. There are echoes of both Graham Greene and Patricia Highsmith here, but Osborne’s sense of place and ability create an undercurrent of menace all his own.

Mad Mabel by Sally Hepworth (Macmillan, £16.99)

The titular character of Australian Hepworth’s latest is a stroppy, sarcastic 81-year-old, living under a pseudonym in a quiet Melbourne suburb. More than 60 years earlier, Mabel Waller became the youngest person in Australian history to be convicted of murder. Now she keeps herself to herself, but Persephone, the lonely young daughter of a neighbour, is determined to be friends, and slowly Mabel, whose own desolate childhood with her wealthy but uninterested parents is gradually revealed in flashbacks, begins to thaw. But someone has discovered her past and is sending anonymous letters, and when the elderly man next door dies unexpectedly, she becomes the prime suspect. Although crime fiction aficionados may figure out at least one plot twist early on, Mabel’s cantankerous facade, behind which the fuzzy outlines of loss, trauma and misunderstanding gradually sharpen into focus, and the growing warmth of the intergenerational friendship, make this a genuinely moving and surprisingly funny read.

entries.title: The Beverly Hills Housewife by James Cahill review – a trip inside Hockney’s world
entries.summary: Muse Betty Freeman sits at the centre of this sun-drenched book about art, eccentricity, and the spirit of Los AngelesDavid Hockney was 29 years old when he came to Betty Freeman’s house to photograph her swimming pool. entries.content:
David Hockney was 29 years old when he came to Betty Freeman’s house to photograph her swimming pool. Scouting locations for the pool paintings that would make him a household name, he took preparatory snaps of his partner, Peter Schlesinger, emerging naked from the water. And yet something about his aloof and quietly eccentric host, who dusted the hunting trophies while a handsome young man padded around her patio in the altogether, intrigued the artist. So he asked whether he might photograph her too, and she agreed.

Completed a year later, Beverly Hills Housewife (1966/7) shows a beautiful woman standing outside a beautiful house. The scene is lit by an unbroken sun, her blond bob is undisturbed by any breeze, a lush fern sets off her popping pink dress. She is surrounded by the symbols of mid-century American prosperity: a chair by Le Corbusier, a tasteful modernist sculpture. We don’t need the title to know the place and time, because Hockney’s paintings have come to define them in our imagination: shimmering water and scattered light, bright colours and reflective surfaces, a clean and impassive contentment.

In this comparably polished mix of anecdote and art history, James Cahill uses Hockney’s painting as a “primary source” for his own multifaceted portrait of the working-class Yorkshireman who fell in love with Los Angeles, of the wealthy art collector who became his friend and ally, and of the city that would go on to shape the culture in which we now live. After potted introductions to these central characters, Cahill starts by unpacking the “lifestyle-magazine version of bourgeois affluence” that Beverly Hills Housewife presents to us.

In doing so, he provides an object lesson in how to read a picture, drawing the reader’s attention to the details that illuminate it. Note, for example, that Freeman’s face is doubled by the stuffed head of an antelope shot by her husband and mounted on the wall. Recast as a cultured woman trapped in a loveless marriage with a conspicuously absent big-game hunter, Freeman’s blank expression comes to seem melancholy rather than merely vacant (that the self-deprecating title was her idea suggests a disillusioned kind of wit). Hockney at his best was a narrative painter, and his pictures invite and are animated by such interpretations.

Yet a portrait always tells us as much about its maker as its muse, and so Cahill moves on to what this painting might reveal of the artist’s own ideas and affinities. Most instructively, he shows how Hockney adopted the compositional model of the annunciation, in which the Virgin Mary receives news of her fate from the angel Gabriel, and painted Freeman into Mary’s place. This allows Cahill to elaborate on the artist’s debt to the early Renaissance masters, and then to speculate on the dynamic between this young, gay man and the glamorous older woman he represents (with gentle irony) as the Madonna: victim and mother, protector and icon. Like all good criticism, the simple observations underpinning these speculations seem so obvious once pointed out that they cannot be unseen, and change the picture for ever.

The difficulty the book runs into is that there is only so much to unpack. Hockney was a painter of enclosed worlds, from which the otherwise inescapable facts of Los Angeles life – the Watts riots, choking smog, Vietnam – are excluded. This does not diminish him as an artist any more than it diminishes Vermeer, and Cahill is justified in arguing that “meaning might reside in so-called veneers” as much as in what lies beneath them. But it does make his work a difficult subject for the kind of ekphrastic exercise that requires hidden layers of meaning to excavate.

So, recognising that Hockney was more interested in the “concealments of portraiture, its feints and deflections” than in exposing any hidden truth, Cahill follows his lead. Rather than digging up the painting’s glossy surface, he glances off it into anecdotal histories of vanguard American music (of which Freeman was an influential supporter), the mythologised Los Angeles art scene (with Edward Kienholz’s darkness as counterpoint to Hockney’s light), and much else besides. There are heroes (the hobo composer Harry Partch) and villains (the painter Clyfford Still, whose egomania and vanity is entertainingly monstrous even when set against the high bar maintained by the abstract expressionist movement).

At times this can feel tendentious, and the connections that link the period back to the painting somewhat strained. But it is testament to the agility of his prose and the lightness of Cahill’s touch that the reader is unlikely to mind, and so this portrait of multiple subjects continues to feel enlightening and engaging long after the painting at its heart has been exhausted. His book is in this respect much like its primary source: charming, clever, and difficult to pin down.

entries.title: Can Nothing Save Us? by Irvine Welsh review – US family saga is a late-career triumph
entries.summary: The Scottish author focuses on gun culture and generational conflict in this darkly satirical tale about a great power in decline“Why expect unconditional love from somebody you’ve brought into a fucked, dying planet, who then has to sit around and watch you screw it up even more?” So muses twentysomething college dropout Luke Ayrton on his parental lineage as he works the Las Vegas Strip, “compin
entries.content:
“Why expect unconditional love from somebody you’ve brought into a fucked, dying planet, who then has to sit around and watch you screw it up even more?” So muses twentysomething college dropout Luke Ayrton on his parental lineage as he works the Las Vegas Strip, “comping girls for clubs” in Sin City. His job is to trawl the “plankton” of bacherlorette parties in order to lure the “whales” – rich men willing to spend to try to impress young women.

“In this game your sociology skills sharpened,” it’s observed, but beyond the seedy side hustle lie weightier concerns: the matter of his family legacy. Electronic dance music aficionado and aspiring writer Luke is estranged from his Maga-positive Mom and Dad, and now lives with grandparents George and Molly, affluent boomers with a countercultural past.

Vietnam vet and retired lawyer George sees himself as a “hippy sellout”, his dream of pursuing human rights advocacy corrupted by real estate deals and entertainment law. Actor Molly’s early theatre and independent cinema success led only to small parts in low-budget film and TV. Grandson Luke is set to inherit their fortune, yet struggles for meaning against a background of disappointment and growing despair: an intergenerational nihilism that deepens like a coastal shelf.

Irvine Welsh’s 16th novel Can Nothing Save Us? comes as something of a surprise. An epic American family saga, it explores a collective emotional malaise at the heart of a great power in decline. This is a bold and ambitious work, in which Welsh deftly shifts point of view with confidence and conviction: his ability to jump generations and to capture the voices and feelings of his disparate cast of characters is at times quite astonishing.

Our author’s way into this garish universe is clearly via his familiarity with the Las Vegas club scene. There’s an early namecheck of Scottish DJ Calvin Harris, friend and collaborator with a long-term residency on the Strip. Welsh’s ear for the demotic is as strong as ever as he conveys the slang and grammar of Luke’s world, as well as the sense of being a small player on the periphery of a bewildering, drug-addled circuit. The theme of generational trench warfare is neatly set up at a legal meeting where Luke’s parents, Gina and Don, are informed of their disinheritance by Molly and George. A standard trope of family drama takes a Rabelaisian turn. “Me grow up?” Gina retorts at maternal accusations of immaturity. “You drink your own urine and walk around naked.” The elderly couple’s “urotherapy” remains a rather desperate last vestige of an alternative lifestyle, perhaps a metaphor for the diminished returns of a dying idealism. Welsh’s knack for absurd social satire is regularly deployed to interrogate serious themes and visit dark places.

In Vietnam, George was a witness to the My Lai massacre, when hundreds of unarmed Vietnamese civilians were murdered by US soldiers. He is also a survivor of a lone gunman’s attack on the Las Vegas Strip from the Mandalay Bay Hotel in 2017. The buried trauma of past atrocities seems to feed a societal yearning for the freedom to bear arms. “The mass-shooting at Mandalay Bay had no long-term impact,” Welsh comments. “White Americans, at least on a conceptual level, didn’t mind being shot at by other white Americans; some even considered it their birthright.”

Facing his own mortality, George excavates the past with his PTSD-ridden fellow veterans, as elsewhere in the land of the free a resigned feeling of rearmament reigns. An anonymous and ultra-disaffected “weapons engineer” is tooling up to settle his score with society. An ayahuasca ceremony at a desert commune descends into gun-toting mayhem. And on a hunting trip planned as a family bonding exercise, Luke finds himself aiming a rifle at his father, Don.

The plot develops a mercilessly ballistic energy of its own as multiple storylines converge on another mass shooting, this time at an outdoor festival called Our Rave’s Electric. A complex and explosive denouement almost succumbs to the chaos it depicts, though in the end the only control on the narrative seems the fateful trajectory of a familiar American tragedy. Its inevitability only makes it all the more pitiful.

We are left with a poignant coda of post-trauma, and a disturbing sense that this is merely part of an unending, generational cycle. Can Nothing Save Us? has apparently had a long gestation period, at one time in development as a TV project. That Welsh has finally realised this story in such an expansive, compelling and heartfelt novel is something of a literary triumph, proof that this medium remains the best kind of long-form narrative. And it’s certainly a late-career tour de force for the author himself.

Jake Arnott’s latest novel is Netherwood (Titan). Can Nothing Save Us? by Irvine Welsh is published by Jonathan Cape (£20). To support the Guardian buy a copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Universality by Natasha Brown audiobook review – a sparkling multi-voiced satire
entries.summary: A magazine article about stolen gold sparks a culture war between a cast of politically polarised charactersA stinging dissection of wealth, class and the media, Natasha Brown’s satire begins with a man named Jake gazing at a gold bar he has found at a farm in West Yorkshire. entries.content:
A stinging dissection of wealth, class and the media, Natasha Brown’s satire begins with a man named Jake gazing at a gold bar he has found at a farm in West Yorkshire. Outside, an illegal rave is taking place which will end in three hospitalisations and property damage. Pondering what to do with the ingot that he has just used to bludgeon a stranger, Jake decides to do a runner.

The story of the stolen gold is told by a journalist, Hannah, in a magazine article named A Fool’s Gold, replicated in full here, which she claims exposes “the fraying fabric of British society, worn thin by late capitalism’s relentless abrasion”. Her piece, which goes viral, features Richard Spencer, an arrogant, philandering banker and the owner of the farm, whose reputation is left in tatters; a contrarian rightwing newspaper columnist named Miriam Leonard, known as Lenny; and a group of radical anarchist squatters who call themselves The Universalists.

Universality goes on to dissect the fallout from the article via the varying perspectives of its protagonists, all of which makes it ideal for the multi-voice audio treatment: Norma Butikofer narrates Hannah’s article while Hannah herself, a burnt-out literary journalist who stumbles on a scoop, is voiced by Anushka Chakravarti. Clare Corbett reads Lenny, antihero of the culture wars, and Daniel Weyman reads from the viewpoint of the self-pitying Richard, who calls Hannah’s actions “a cruel confidence trick”. Though we come to understand that each of the characters has an axe to grind; which of them, if any, can we trust?

Further listening

The Calamity Club

Kathryn Stockett, Penguin Audio, 28hr 45min

Meg, a young orphan deemed “unadoptable”, has her fortunes changed when she meets Birdie, the new bookkeeper at her orphanage. This Depression-era novel from the author of The Help is read by January LaVoy and Jenna Lamia.

It Could Have Been Her

Lisa Jewell, Penguin Audio, 10hr 47min

Lesley Sharp, James Norton, Emila Fox and Tim McInnerny are among the cast reading this new thriller from the None of This Is True author. A woman goes on a voyage into her past after a stray dog turns up on her doorstep and she sets about trying to find its owner.

entries.title: EJ Swift wins the 2026 Arthur C Clarke award for science fiction
entries.summary: The writer – who was also shortlisted in 2023 – has won the prize for her book When There Are Wolves Again, a speculative work of eco-fiction set in near-future Britain A novel about rewilding and climate activism in Britain has been named this year’s winner of the Arthur C Clarke award for science fiction.When There Are Wolves Again by EJ Swift is an “ambitious study in the power of long-term hop
entries.content:
A novel about rewilding and climate activism in Britain has been named this year’s winner of the Arthur C Clarke award for science fiction.

When There Are Wolves Again by EJ Swift is an “ambitious study in the power of long-term hope in the face of climate breakdown”, said the award’s director, Tom Hunter.

The award, now in its 40th year, is given each year to “the best science fiction novel” first published in the UK in the previous year. It was named after British author Arthur C Clarke, who gave a grant to establish the award in 1987. Swift receives £2,026 in prize money, in keeping with the award’s tradition of increasing it incrementally each year since 2001.

When There Are Wolves Again follows two women across half a century in a near-future Britain. Lucy, whose childhood is shaped by the Covid lockdowns, becomes involved in climate activism and campaigns to revive Britain’s habitats, while Hester is a documentary-maker whose life was marked by the Chornobyl disaster. Their separate journeys eventually converge in 2070.

This year, judges considered a record 132 books submitted by 52 UK publishing imprints and independent authors.

In her Guardian review, Lisa Tuttle described the winning novel as “evocative and beautifully written”, praising it as a “character-driven … argument for rewilding in Britain”. Like Swift’s previous novel, The Coral Bones, she wrote, the book is “powered by a passionate love of nature and deep concern for the planet’s future”.

Judging chair Dr Andrew M Butler, a critic and academic, called it “a story of environmental change and possible recovery”.

Hunter added: “Science fiction at its most powerful is often not about predicting the future but showing us that no one future has to be inevitable.”

Swift was chosen as the winner over five other shortlisted authors: Matt Dinniman for Dungeon Crawler Carl, Laila Lalami for The Dream Hotel, Silvia Park for Luminous, qntm for There Is No Antimemetics Division and Lorraine Wilson for The Salt Oracle.

Swift’s previous novels include The Coral Bones, which was also shortlisted for the Arthur C Clarke award and the British Science Fiction Association award for best novel. She is also the author of the time-travel novel Paris Adrift and the Osiris Project trilogy, which explores the geopolitical impacts of environmental breakdown. She cites writers including Margaret Atwood, Barbara Kingsolver, Kim Stanley Robinson and Emily St John Mandel among her influences.

Clarke wrote about 100 works of science fiction and nonfiction, and also co-wrote the screenplay for the 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

Margaret Atwood won the inaugural Arthur C Clarke prize in 1987 for The Handmaid’s Tale. Subsequent winners include Colson Whitehead’s The Underground Railroad (in 2017) and Emily St John Mandel’s Station Eleven (in 2015). Last year, US author Sierra Greer won for Annie Bot, a novel told from the perspective of a robot girlfriend.

Butler was joined on the judging panel by film and translation scholar Eliza Claudia Filimon, writer Antony Jones, novelist and editor Tiffani Angus, space physicist John Coxon, and games studies professor Esther MacCallum-Stewart.

When There Are Wolves Again by E. J. Swift (Quercus Publishing, £10.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.
